quote: Wenn ich $s$ mal mit der Hand Sand greife wie {+$s_d$+} oft{+!+} kommt es vor, dass die Abweichung d.h. die Differenz der schwarzen u. weissen Körner $d$ ist? $s_d = s(d)$?
english: If I grab sand with my hand $s$ times, how often ($s_d$ times!) does it happen that the deviation, i.e. the difference between the black and white grains, is $d$? $s_d = s(d)$?
topic: Statistical mechanics: deriving the most probable velocity distribution of molecules via Lagrange multipliers, then asking for the most probable distribution of an ensemble of systems over distributions, with an analogy to drawing black and white grains of sand, and a closing plan to study collision forces in Mie–Born electrodynamics.

triage.modern_statement: Take a handful of n grains s times. Each grain is independently black or white with probability 1/2. The question is the expected number s_d of handfuls in which (#black − #white) = d. Since d = 2k − n with k ~ Binomial(n, 1/2), s_d = s·C(n,(n+d)/2)/2^n. For large n this is approximately s·√(2/(πn))·exp(−d²/(2n)) (taking only d with the same parity as n), which is a Gaussian law for the deviation. In other words, it is the distribution of a simple symmetric random walk after n steps. Hilbert is using this as an example to motivate the 'most probable distribution' of an ensemble.
triage.answered_by: This is a classical result that predates Hilbert. Abraham de Moivre gave the normal approximation to the binomial in 1733 (an unpublished pamphlet) and in The Doctrine of Chances (1738). Laplace later extended it, giving the de Moivre–Laplace theorem. The exact answer is the binomial distribution (Jacob Bernoulli). This is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: De Moivre gave an approximation to the binomial distribution in 1733, first in an unpublished pamphlet and then in The Doctrine of Chances (1738).
In 1733 Abraham de Moivre presented an approximation to the binomial distribution, i.e. the normal approximation to the binomial.
The de Moivre–Laplace theorem relates the binomial distribution to the normal distribution as n tends to infinity.

triage.why: The note asks for the frequency distribution of the black-minus-white difference over repeated random handfuls. That is the binomial distribution, and the de Moivre–Laplace theorem gives its Gaussian limit. Both were standard well before Hilbert's time. On the page it is a teaching or heuristic analogy for ensemble statistics in statistical mechanics, not a new research question. It is not on any list of Hilbert's published problems. The modern formula is my own reconstruction, assuming a 50/50 color mix and a fixed handful size n; Hilbert's note gives neither. The sources cited only support the history of the binomial normal approximation; none of them discusses Hilbert's notebook.
